Momentum equals mass times velocity: \(\mathbf p=m\mathbf v\). Here \(\mathbf p\) denotes momentum, a symbol seldom used in A level Mathematics. Its direction is the direction of the velocity.
Its units are \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\) or \(\mathrm{N\,s}\). These are equivalent because \(F=ma\) gives \(1\;\mathrm N=1\;\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}\).

parts.text: Fill in the gaps in the table below
(if possible give momentum as a vector, otherwise find the magnitude of momentum.

transcription.tex: For a constant force, impulse equals force multiplied by the time for which it acts.

shapes.alt: A strongman pulling an aeroplane with a harness

transcription.tex: The momentum gained by the aeroplane depends on how hard the man pulls and how long he pulls for.

The impulse–momentum principle: \(\mathbf I=\mathbf F t=m\mathbf a t\).\par Substituting \(\mathbf a=(\mathbf v-\mathbf u)/t\) gives \(\mathbf I=m(\mathbf v-\mathbf u)=m\mathbf v-m\mathbf u\).\par Impulse is the change in momentum, so both have units \(\mathrm{N\,s}\).
When a very large force acts for a very short time, as a bat strikes a ball, the change in momentum is often easier to calculate than the force and contact time.
Tip: Choose a positive direction first. A velocity in the opposite direction has a negative sign.
Calculate the impulse exerted on the object in the following cases:
1. A force of 30N is exerted on an object for 0.5s
2. A ball of mass 3kg was travelling at 10m/s is hit and slows to 6m/s without changing direction.
3. A ball of mass 3kg was travelling at 10m/s is hit so that it returns in the opposite direction at a speed of 6m/s
4. A rocket of mass 100kg travelling at 2000m/s hits the ground and stops.
5. The momentum before impact is 6i + 3j Ns and the momentum after impact is 10i + 5j Ns
\((10-6)\mathbf i+(5-3)\mathbf j=4\mathbf i+2\mathbf j\;\mathrm{N\,s}\)
6. The momentum before impact is 6i - 5j Ns and the momentum after impact is 10i + 5j Ns
\((10-6)\mathbf i+(5+5)\mathbf j=4\mathbf i+10\mathbf j\;\mathrm{N\,s}\)

For the balls and rocket, take the initial direction of motion as positive. A negative impulse acts against that direction. Reversing direction gives a larger impulse magnitude than slowing by the same amount.

[Textbook] A ball of mass 0.2 kg hits a vertical wall at right angles with a speed of 3.5 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The ball rebounds with speed 2.5 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the magnitude of the impulse exerted on the wall by the ball.
A stationary wall can receive an impulse. Its support keeps it at rest, so its change of momentum alone cannot give the contact impulse. Neither the contact force nor the contact time is known.

Take motion towards the wall as positive. For the ball, \(u=+3.5\) and \(v=-2.5\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).\par \(I_{\rm ball}=m(v-u)=0.2(-2.5-3.5)=-1.2\;\mathrm{N\,s}.\)\par By Newton’s third law the impulse on the wall is equal and opposite. Its magnitude is \(1.2\;\mathrm{N\,s}\).
Edexcel M1 Jun 2007 Q2a

Two particles A and B, of mass 0.3 kg and m kg respectively, are moving in opposite directions along the same straight horizontal line so that the particles collide directly. Immediately before the collision, the speeds of A and B are 8 m s \(^{-1}\) and 4 m s \(^{-1}\) respectively. In the collision the direction of motion of each particle is reversed and, immediately after the collision, the speed of each particle is 2 m s \(^{-1}\).\par Find\par (a) the magnitude of the impulse exerted by B on A in the collision,\par [3 marks]

Take the initial direction of A as positive. Its velocity changes from \(+8\) to \(-2\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).\par Impulse on A equals its change of momentum: \(I_A=m_A(v_A-u_A)\). [M1]\par \(I_A=0.3(-2-8)=-3\;\mathrm{N\,s}\). [A1]\par The impulse is opposite to A’s initial motion. Its magnitude is \(3\;\mathrm{N\,s}\). [A1]
Question 4

A ball of mass 0.2 kg, moving along a horizontal surface, hits a fixed vertical wall at right angles. The ball rebounds at right angles to the wall with speed \(3.5\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\). Given that the magnitude of the impulse exerted on the ball by the wall is 2Ns, find the speed of the ball just before it hits the wall. [3 marks]

Take the direction away from the wall as positive. If the incoming speed is \(u\), the velocities before and after are \(-u\) and \(+3.5\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).\par The wall gives the ball an impulse of \(+2\;\mathrm{N\,s}\). Use \(I=m(v-u_{\rm initial})\). [M1]\par \(2=0.2[3.5-(-u)]\), hence \(10=3.5+u\). [A1]\par The incoming speed was \(u=6.5\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). [A1]
Question 5

A ball of mass 0.2 kg is dropped from a height of 2.5m above horizontal ground. After hitting the ground it bounces to a height of 1.8m above the ground. Find the magnitude of the impulse received by the ball from the ground. [4 marks]

Before the bounce, take downwards as positive. The ball starts from rest and falls \(2.5\,\mathrm m\): \(u=0,\;a=g,\;s=2.5\).\par \(v^2=u^2+2as=0^2+2(9.8)(2.5)=49\), so the impact speed is \(7\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) downwards. [M1]

After the bounce, take upwards as positive. The ball rises \(1.8\,\mathrm m\) and comes instantaneously to rest: \(v=0,\;a=-g,\;s=1.8\).\par \(0=u^2+2(-9.8)(1.8)\), so \(u^2=35.28\) and the rebound speed is \(5.94\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). [M1]
Using upwards as positive for both velocities at impact, \(I=0.2[5.94-(-7)]=2.588\;\mathrm{N\,s}\) [M1]. The impulse magnitude is \(2.59\;\mathrm{N\,s}\) [A1] (2 d.p.).

slides.title: The law of Conservation of Momentum

parts.text: The law of Conservation of Momentum
1. An isolated system is a collection of bodies which only experience unbalanced forces from other bodies in the system.
Velocities: use single arrows detached from bodies
Impulses: use arrows attached to bodies (like forces)
is equal on both bodies (equal and opposite forces acting for equal time).
Calculated the value of the unknown in the following isolated systems.
All velocities marked are in m/s and all masses in kg.

transcription.tex: [Textbook] Two particles P and Q, of masses 8kg and 2kg respectively, are connected by a light inextensible string. The particles are at rest on a smooth horizontal plane with the string slack. Particle P is projected directly away from Q with speed \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).\par Find the common speed of the particles after the string goes taut.\par Find the magnitude of the impulse transmitted through the string when it goes taut.

Take left as positive. The string transmits an internal impulse, so total horizontal momentum is conserved. Both particles move at speed \(v\) when the string becomes taut.\par \(8(4)+2(0)=(8+2)v\), so \(v=3.2\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
For Q, \(I_Q=m_Q(v-u)=2(3.2-0)=6.4\;\mathrm{N\,s}\) to the left. The impulse on P has the same magnitude and acts to the right.
Edexcel M1 Jan 2014 (I) Q1

A truck P of mass 2M is moving with speed U on smooth straight horizontal rails. It collides directly with another truck Q of mass 3M which is moving with speed 4U in the opposite direction on the same rails. The trucks join so that immediately after the collision they move together. By modelling the trucks as particles, find\par (a) the speed of the trucks immediately after the collision.\par [3 marks]\par (b) the magnitude of the impulse exerted on P by Q in the collision.\par [3 marks]

(a) Take Q’s initial direction as positive. Conservation of momentum gives \(2M(-U)+3M(4U)=(2M+3M)V\). [M1] [A1]\par \(10MU=5MV\), so the trucks move together with speed \(2U\) in Q’s initial direction. [A1]

(b) The impulse on P equals its change of momentum: \(I_P=2M(V-(-U))\). [M1]\par Substitute \(V=2U\): \(I_P=2M(2U+U)\). [A1] Its magnitude is \(6MU\). [A1]\par Check using Q: \(I_Q=3M(2U-4U)=-6MU\), equal and opposite.
Question 5

Two particles A and B of masses 2 kg and 5 kg respectively are moving towards each other along the same straight line on a smooth horizontal surface. The particles collide. Before the collision the speeds of A and B are \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) and \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) respectively. After the collision the direction of motion of A is reversed and its speed is \(1.5\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\). Find:\par \textbf{a)} the speed and direction of B after the collision [3 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the magnitude of the impulse given by A to B in the collision. [3 marks]

\textbf{a)} Conservation of momentum \(\rightarrow\)) [M1]\par \((2 \times 6)+(5 \times(-4))=(2 \times(-1.5))+5 v\)\par \(12-20=-3+5 v\)\par \(-5=5 v\)\par \(v=-1\) [A1]\par The speed of B is 1 m s \(^{-1}\) and its direction of motion is unchanged by the collision. [A1]\par \textbf{b)} For \(A:(\leftarrow) I=2(1.5-(-6))\) [M1]\par \(=2 \times 7.5\)\par \(=15\) [A1]
[or for \(B:(\rightarrow) I=5(v-(-4))\)\par \(=5(-1+4)\)\par \(=15\)]\par The magnitude of the impulse given to B is 15 N s [A1]
Question 6

A particle P of mass 150 g is at rest on a smooth horizontal plane. A second particle Q of mass 100 g is projected along the plane with speed \(u\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and collides directly with P. On impact the particles join together and move on with speed \(4\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Find the value of u. [4 marks]
Conservation of momentum \((\rightarrow)\) [M1]\par \(100 u+\left( 150 \times0\right)=250 \times4\) [M1] [A1]\par \(100 u=1000\)\par \(u=10\) [A1]\par The value of u is 10.
Question 7

A particle A of mass 4m is moving along a smooth horizontal surface with speed 2u. It collides with another particle B of mass 3m which is moving with the same speed along the same straight line but in the opposite direction. Given that A is brought to rest by the collision, find:\par \textbf{a)} the velocity of B after the collision [3 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the magnitude of the impulse given by A to B in the collision. [3 marks]

Conservation of momentum \((\rightarrow)\)\par \((4m \times 2u) + (3m \times (-2u)) = (4m \times 0) + (3m \times v)\) [M1] [A1]\par \(8mu - 6mu = 3mv\)\par \(2mu = 3mv\)\par \(v = \frac{2u}{3}\)\par The velocity of \(B\) after the collision is \(\frac{2u}{3}\) m s\(^{-1}\) in the opposite direction. [A1]\par \textbf{b)} For \(A:(\leftarrow) I = 4m(0 - (-2u))\) [M1] [A1]\par \(= 8mu\)
The magnitude of the impulse given by \(A\) to \(B\) is \(8mu\) [A1]\par [or for \(B:(\rightarrow) I = 3m(v - (-2u))\)
\(= 3m\left(\frac{2u}{3} + 2u\right)\)
Question 8

An explosive charge of mass 150 g is designed to split into two parts, one with mass 100 g and the other with mass 50 g. When the charge is moving at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) it splits and the larger part continues to move in the same direction whilst the smaller part moves in the opposite direction. Given that the speed of the larger part is twice the speed of the smaller part, find the speeds of each of the two parts. [3 marks]

\(( 150 \times4)=( 100 \times2 u)+( 50 \times(-u))\) [M1] [A1]\par \(600=200 u-50 u\)\par \(600=150 u\)\par \(4=u\)\par The larger has speed \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) and the smaller part has speed \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) [A1]
Question 9

Two particles P and Q of masses m and km respectively are moving towards each other in opposite directions along the same straight line on a smooth horizontal surface. The particles collide. Before the collision the speeds of P and Q are 3u and u respectively. After the collision the direction of motion of both particles is reversed and the speed of each particle is halved.\par \textbf{a)} Find the value of k. [4 marks]\par \textbf{b)} Find, in terms of m and u, the magnitude of the impulse given by P to Q in the collision. [3 marks]

\textbf{a)} Conservation of momentum \((\rightarrow)\) [M1]\par \((m\times 3 u)+(k m\times(-u))=\left(m\times\frac{-3 u}{2}\right)+\left(k m\times\frac{u}{2}\right)\) [A1]\par \(3 m u-k m u=-\frac{3 m u}{2}+\frac{k m u}{2}\)\par \(6-2 k=-3+k\) [M1]\par \(3=k\) [A1]\par The value of k is 3.\par \textbf{b)} For \(P:(\leftarrow) I=m\left(\frac{3 u}{2}-(-3 u)\right)\) [M1] [or for \(Q:(\rightarrow) I=k m\left(\frac{u}{2}-(-u)\right)\) [A1]
\(=\frac{9 m u}{2}\)\par \(=3 m \times\frac{3 u}{2}\)\par \(=\frac{9 m u}{2} ]\)
The magnitude of the impulse is \(\frac{9 m u}{2}\) [A1]
Question 10

Two particles A and B of masses 4 kg and 2 kg respectively are connected by a light inextensible string. The particles are at rest on a smooth horizontal plane with the string slack. Particle A is projected directly away from B with speed \(u\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\). When the string goes taut the impulse transmitted through the string has magnitude 6Ns. Find:\par \textbf{a)} the common speed of the particles just after the string goes taut [4 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the value of u. [3 marks]

10a For \(B:(\rightarrow)\)\par impulse-momentum principle [M1]\par \(6=2(v-0)\) [M1] [A1]\par \(3=v\)\par The common speed is \(3\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) [A1]\par \textbf{b)} Conservation of momentum \((\rightarrow)\) [M1]\par \(4u=2v+4v=6\times 3=18\) [A1]\par \(u=4.5\)\par [or impulse-momentum principle for \(A\)\par \((\rightarrow)-6=4(3-u)\)
\(-1.5=3-u\)\par \(u=4.5\) ]\par The value of u is 4.5. [A1]
Question 11

Two particles P and Q of masses 3 kg and 2 kg respectively are moving along the same straight line on a smooth horizontal surface. The particles collide. After the collision both the particles are moving in the same direction, the speed of P is \(1\,\mathrm{~m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and the speed of Q is \(1.5\,\mathrm{~m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}.\) The magnitude of the impulse of P on Q is 9Ns. Find:\par \textbf{a)} the speed and direction of P before the collision [3 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the speed and direction of Q before the collision. [3 marks]

\textbf{a)} For \(P\): \(\leftarrow\) impulse-momentum principle [M1]\par \(9=3(-1-(-u))\) [A1]\par \(9=3(-1+u)\)\par \(3=-1+u\)\par \(4=u\)\par The speed of \(P\) before the collision is 4 m s \(^{-1}\) and it was moving in the same direction as it was after the collision. [A1]\par \textbf{b)} For \(Q\): \(\rightarrow\) impulse-momentum principle [M1]\par \(9=2(1.5-v)\) [A1]
[or conservation of momentum \(\rightarrow\) ]\par \(3u+2v=(3\times 1)+(2\times 1.5)\)
\(12+2v=3+3=6\)\par \(2v=-6\)\par \(v=-3\)]\par The speed of \(Q\) before the collision was 3 m s \(^{-1}\) and it was moving in the opposite direction to its direction after the collision. [A1]
Question 12

Two particles A and B are moving in the same direction along the same straight line on a smooth horizontal surface. The particles collide. Before the collision the speed of B is \(1.5\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}.\) After the collision the direction of motion of both particles is unchanged, the speed of A is \(2.5\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) and the speed of B is \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}.\) Given that the mass of A is three times the mass of B,\par \textbf{a)} find the speed of A before the collision. [4 marks]\par Given that the magnitude of the impulse on A in the collision is 3 Ns,\par \textbf{b)} find the mass of A. [3 marks]
\(3 m u+1.5 m=(3 m \times2.5)+(m \times3)\) [M1] [A1]\par \(3 m u+1.5 m=7.5 m+3 m\)\par \(3 u=9\) [M1]\par \(u=3\)\par The speed of A before the collision is \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) [A1]

\textbf{b)} Using the impulse-momentum principle:\par for \(B:(\rightarrow)\)\par \(3=m(3-1.5)\) [M1]\par \(2=m\) [A1]\par [or for \(A:(\leftarrow)\)\par \(3=3 m(-2.5-(-u))\)\par \(3=3 m(-2.5+3)\)\par \(1=0.5 m\)\par \(2=m ]\)\par The mass of A is 6 kg. [A1]

Mass and time are scalars. Momentum, force, velocity and impulse are vectors. In one dimension a sign gives the direction. In two or three dimensions, apply the impulse equation separately to each component.

A particle of mass 0.2 kg is moving with velocity \((10\mathbf i-5\mathbf j)\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) when it receives an impulse \((3\mathbf i-2\mathbf j)\;\mathrm{N\,s}\). Find the new velocity of the particle.

Impulse is change in momentum: \(\mathbf I=m(\mathbf v-\mathbf u)\).\par Substitute the known impulse, mass and initial velocity:\par \(3\mathbf i-2\mathbf j=0.2[\mathbf v-(10\mathbf i-5\mathbf j)]\).\par Divide both components by 0.2 to find the change in velocity:\par \(15\mathbf i-10\mathbf j=\mathbf v-(10\mathbf i-5\mathbf j)\).\par Add the initial velocity and collect like components:\par \(\mathbf v=(10+15)\mathbf i+(-5-10)\mathbf j=(25\mathbf i-15\mathbf j)\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
Use Pythagoras to find the magnitude of a vector such as momentum or impulse. Use trigonometry and the signs of its components to find the direction.
Tip: Speed is the magnitude of velocity. Distance is the magnitude of displacement for motion in one direction along a straight line.

An ice hockey puck of mass 0.17 kg receives an impulse \(\mathbf Q\;\mathrm{N\,s}\). Immediately before the impulse the velocity of the puck is \((10\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and immediately afterwards its velocity is \((15\mathbf i-7\mathbf j)\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the magnitude of \(\mathbf Q\) and the angle between \(\mathbf Q\) and \(\mathbf i\).

\(\mathbf Q=m(\mathbf v-\mathbf u)\)\par \(=0.17[(15\mathbf i-7\mathbf j)-(10\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)]\)\par \(=0.85\mathbf i-2.04\mathbf j\;\mathrm{N\,s}\).\par Magnitude: \(|\mathbf Q|=\sqrt{0.85^2+2.04^2}=2.21\;\mathrm{N\,s}\).\par The positive horizontal and negative vertical components place the vector below the positive \(\mathbf i\) axis.\par \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(2.04/0.85)=67.4^\circ\) (1 d.p.), clockwise from \(\mathbf i\).
Tip: Sketch the components before deciding which angle to report.
Edexcel M2 · January 2012 · Question 1

A tennis ball of mass 0.1 kg is hit by a racquet. Immediately before being hit, the ball has velocity \(30 \mathrm{i} \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}\). The racquet exerts an impulse of \((-2 \mathrm{i}-4 \mathrm{j})\) N s on the ball. By modelling the ball as a particle, find the velocity of the ball immediately after being hit.

Impulse equals the change in momentum.\par \(m(\mathbf v-\mathbf u)=\mathbf I\).\par Substitute the mass, initial velocity and impulse:\par \(0.1(\mathbf v-30\mathbf i)=-2\mathbf i-4\mathbf j\).\par Rearrange to isolate the final momentum:\par \(0.1\mathbf v=3\mathbf i-2\mathbf i-4\mathbf j=\mathbf i-4\mathbf j\).\par Divide both components by 0.1:\par \(\mathbf v=(10\mathbf i-40\mathbf j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
Question 11

A cricket ball of mass 0.5 kg is hit by a bat. Immediately before being hit the velocity of the ball is \(( 20 \mathbf{i}-4 \mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) and immediately afterwards it is \((- 16 \mathbf{i}+8 \mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\). Find the magnitude of the impulse exerted on the ball by the bat. [3 marks]

Impulse \(=\) change in momentum\par \(= m\mathbf{v}-m\mathbf{u}\)\par \(= 0.5 \times(-16 \mathbf{i}+8 \mathbf{j})-0.5 \times(20 \mathbf{i}-4 \mathbf{j})\) [M1]\par \(= -8 \mathbf{i}+4 \mathbf{j}-10 \mathbf{i}+2 \mathbf{j}\)\par \(= -18 \mathbf{i}+6 \mathbf{j}\) [A1]\par \(\therefore\) Magnitude of the impulse \(= \sqrt{(-18)^{2}+6^{2}}=6\sqrt{10}\)\par \(= 19.0\,\mathrm{N\,s} (3\,\mathrm{s}. \mathrm{f}.)\) [A1]
Question 12

A ball of mass 0.2 kg is hit by a bat. Immediately before being hit by the bat the velocity of the ball is \(- 15 \mathbf{i}\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and the bat exerts an impulse of \(( 2 \mathbf{i}+6 \mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{s}\) on the ball. Find the velocity of the ball after the impact. [3 marks]

Use impulse \(=\) change in momentum\par \(2 \mathbf{i}+6 \mathbf{j}=0.2 \mathbf{v}-0.2 (-15 \mathbf{i})\) [M1]\par \(= 0.2 \mathbf{v}+3 \mathbf{i}\)\par \(\therefore 0.2 \mathbf{v}=2 \mathbf{i}+6 \mathbf{j}-3 \mathbf{i}\)\par \(= -\mathbf{i}+6 \mathbf{j}\) [A1]\par \(\therefore \mathbf{v}=-5 \mathbf{i}+30 \mathbf{j}\) [A1]\par The velocity of the ball after the impact is \((-5 \mathbf{i}+30 \mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\)
Question 13

A particle of mass 0.25 kg has velocity \(\mathbf{v}\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) at time t s where \(\mathbf{v}=(t^{2}-3)\mathbf{i}+4t\mathbf{j}, t\leqslant 3.\)\par When \(t=3\), the particle receives an impulse of \((2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})\) N s. Find the velocity of the particle immediately after the impulse. [3 marks]

\(\mathbf{v}=(t^{2}-3)\mathbf{i}+4t\mathbf{j}\)\par When \(t=3\) let \(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}\)\par \(\mathbf{u}=6\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j}\) [B1]\par Substitute \(t=3\) into the expression for velocity, to find the velocity before the impact.\par Use \(\text{impulse}=\text{change in momentum}\).\par Then \(2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}=0.25\mathbf{v}-0.25(6\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j})\) [M1]\par \(\therefore 0.25\mathbf{v}=2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+0.25(6\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j})\)\par \(=3.5\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}\)\par \(\therefore\quad\mathbf{v}=14\mathbf{i}+20\mathbf{j}\) [A1]
The velocity of the particle after the impulse is \((14\mathbf{i}+20\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\)
Question 14

A ball of mass 2 kg is initially moving with a velocity of \(\left( \mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \right)\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\). It receives an impulse of \(2\mathbf{j}\,\mathrm{N\,s}\). Find the velocity immediately after the impulse and the angle through which the ball is deflected as a result. Give your answer to the nearest degree. [5 marks]

Use impulse \(=\) change in momentum.\par \(2 \mathbf{j}=2 \mathbf{v}-2(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})\) [M1]\par \(\therefore 2 \mathbf{v}=2 \mathbf{j}+2(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})\)\par \(= 2 \mathbf{i}+4 \mathbf{j}\)\par \(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{i}+2 \mathbf{j}\) [A1]\par Immediately after the impulse the velocity is \((\mathbf{i}+2 \mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\)

Before impact the velocity was \(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}\) and so the direction of the ball was at an angle \(\alpha\) with \(\mathbf{i}\), where \(\tan \alpha=\frac{1}{1}\), i.e. \(\alpha=45^{\circ}\) [M1]\par After impact the velocity is \(\mathbf{i}+2 \mathbf{j}\) and so the direction of the ball is at an angle \(\beta\) with \(\mathbf{i}\), where \(\tan \beta=\frac{2}{1}\), i.e. \(\beta=63.4^{\circ}\) [A1]
\(\therefore\) The ball is deflected through an angle of \(63.4-45 \approx18^{\circ}\) (nearest degree). [A1]
Question 15

A particle of mass 0.5 kg moving with velocity \(3 \mathbf{i}\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) collides with a particle of mass 0.25 kg moving with velocity \(12 \mathbf{i}\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). The two particles coalesce and move as one particle of mass 0.75 kg. Find the velocity of the combined particle. [3 marks]

Let the new velocity be \(x\mathbf{i}\) and use conservation of momentum.\par Equate i components to find x.\par Using conservation of momentum: [M1]\par \((0.5\times 3\mathbf{i})+(0.25\times 12\mathbf{i})=0.75x\mathbf{i}\) [A1]\par \(1.5\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{i}=0.75x\mathbf{i}\)\par \(\therefore 0.75x\mathbf{i}=4.5\mathbf{i}\)\par \(x=\frac{4.5}{0.75}\)\par \(=6\)\par So the velocity of the combined particle is \(6\mathbf{i}\) m s \(^{-1}\) [A1]
Question 16

A particle of mass 5 kg moving with velocity \(\left( \mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}\right)\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) collides with a particle of mass 2 kg moving with velocity \(\left(-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}\right)\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\). The two particles coalesce and move as one particle of mass 7 kg. Find the magnitude of the velocity \(\mathbf{v}\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) of the combined particle. [3 marks]

Let the new velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) be \(x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}\)\par Use conservation of momentum:\par \(5(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})+2(-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})=7(x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j})\) [M1]\par \(5\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}=7x\mathbf{i}+7y\mathbf{j}\)\par \(3\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}=7x\mathbf{i}+7y\mathbf{j}\)\par Equate coefficients of \(\mathbf{i}\) and \(\mathbf{j}\) to give\par \(7x=3\) and \(7y=-3\)\par \(\therefore x=\frac{3}{7}\) and \(y=-\frac{3}{7}\)\par \(\therefore\) velocity is \(\frac{3}{7}\mathbf{i}-\frac{3}{7}\mathbf{j}\) [A1]
The magnitude of the velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) is \(\sqrt{\left(\frac{3}{7}\right)^{2}+\left(-\frac{3}{7}\right)^{2}}=\frac{3}{7}\sqrt{2}\) [A1]
